title: The Troubles
wiki_lead:
The Troubles (Irish: Na Trioblóidí) were an ethno-nationalist conflict in Northern Ireland that lasted from the late 1960s to 1998. Also known internationally as the Northern Ireland conflict, it is usually deemed to have ended with the Good Friday Agreement of 1998. Although centred in Northern Ireland, violence at times spilled into the Republic of Ireland, England, and mainland Europe. The conflict arose from political and nationalistic disputes with a strong ethnic and sectarian dimension. Unionists and loyalists, mostly Ulster Protestants, wanted Northern Ireland to remain in the United Kingdom, while Irish nationalists and republicans, mostly Irish Catholics, wanted it to join a united Ireland. Despite the division between Protestants and Catholics, it was not a religious war.
Tensions escalated during a campaign by the Northern Ireland Civil Rights Association to end discrimination against the Catholic‑nationalist minority. The government attempted to suppress the protests, and the Royal Ulster Constabulary (RUC) was criticised for sectarianism and police brutality. Loyalists opposed the campaign, believing it was a front for republican activity. The August 1969 riots led to the deployment of British troops, in what became the British Army's longest operation. "Peace walls" were built to separate communities, and Catholic support for the Army declined after Bloody Sunday in 1972. The main participants included republican paramilitaries such as the Provisional IRA and INLA, loyalist paramilitaries such as the UVF and UDA, British state forces including the British Army and RUC, and political activists. The conflict involved guerrilla and bombing campaigns, sectarian tit‑for‑tat violence, feuds within and between paramilitary groups, counterinsurgency operations, incidents of collusion, riots, mass protests, civil disobedience, and the creation of temporary no‑go areas.
More than 3,500 people were killed, of whom 52% were civilians, 32% were members of the British security forces, and 16% were members of paramilitary groups. Republican paramilitaries were responsible for 60% of total deaths, loyalist paramilitaries for 30%, and security forces for 10%. Loyalists were responsible for 48% of civilian deaths, republicans for 39%, and security forces for 10%. The Northern Ireland peace process led to paramilitary ceasefires and talks between the main political parties, resulting in the Good Friday Agreement of 1998. It restored self‑governance on the basis of "power‑sharing" and included the principle of consent, civil and political rights, parity of esteem, police reform, paramilitary disarmament, and early release of prisoners. Sporadic violence has continued, including punishment attacks, loyalist gangs' control of organised crime, and violent crime linked to dissident republican groups.

The word "troubles" has been used as a synonym for violent conflict for centuries. It was used to describe the 17th-century Wars of the Three Kingdoms
grok_lead: The Troubles was a thirty-year ethno-nationalist conflict in Northern Ireland from 1968 to 1998, characterized by guerrilla warfare, bombings, sectarian assassinations, and riots between Irish republican paramilitaries seeking unification with the Republic of Ireland, Ulster loyalist paramilitaries defending the constitutional link with the United Kingdom, and British security forces attempting to maintain order. The violence resulted in over 3,600 deaths and more than 30,000 injuries, with republican paramilitaries responsible for 59 percent of fatalities, loyalist groups for 28 percent, and state forces for 11 percent. Rooted in partition-era grievances and discrimination against the Catholic minority, the conflict ignited amid 1960s civil rights marches protesting gerrymandering, housing inequities, and electoral barriers in the Protestant-dominated statelet. The primary republican actor, the Provisional Irish Republican Army (PIRA), conducted a sustained terrorist campaign including urban bombings and rural ambushes against military and civilian targets across Northern Ireland and mainland Britain. Loyalist counterparts, such as the Ulster Volunteer Force and Ulster Defence Association, retaliated with targeted killings of suspected nationalists and random sectarian attacks, often in urban enclaves like Belfast's Shankill and Falls roads. British troops, initially deployed in 1969 as peacekeepers, evolved into a counter-insurgency force amid escalating atrocities, including events like Bloody Sunday in 1972 where paratroopers killed 13 unarmed protesters. The era's defining features encompassed internment without trial, hunger strikes that galvanized republican support, and political maneuvering by parties like Sinn FÃ©in and the Democratic Unionist Party. Ceasefires in 1994 paved the way for the 1998 Good Friday Agreement, which devolved power-sharing governance and largely quelled paramilitary activity, though sporadic dissident violence and unresolved legacy issues persist. The conflict's toll extended beyond statistics, entrenching segregation, economic stagnation, and generational trauma in a society divided by identity and allegiance.
